title: Descaling psoriasis narratives on TikTok: A cross-sectional study
screen_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of the first 200 #Psoriasis TikTok videos (134 after exclusions); the 47 educational videos were judged against NICE psoriasis guidance and NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries, and 21 (about 45%) were deemed unreliable. That is a share of items judged discordant with clinical guidance, which the author explicitly calls misinformation/misleading content.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language TikTok videos; author based in the UK and reliability judged against UK NICE guidance)
estimates.date: Not stated; sources consulted May 2024, article received 1 July 2024
estimates.measure_type: % of educational psoriasis TikTok videos judged unreliable against NICE guidance
estimates.value_raw: 21/47 educational videos ('of the 47 educational videos, around 55% (n = 26) were classed as reliable whilst the remaining 45% (n = 21) were deemed unreliable')
estimates.denominator: 47 educational videos, among the 134 English-language #Psoriasis videos analysed (first 200 videos in the hashtag feed, minus 65 non-English and 1 off-topic)
estimates.definition: For educational content only, the information shared was compared with NICE psoriasis guidance (CG153) and NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries and classed reliable or unreliable; unreliable videos were mainly health/wellness gurus advising discontinuation of prescribed medication in favour of dietary change
estimates.misinfo_def: Specifically for educational content, we used the NICE guidelines and NICE clinical knowledge summaries to determine whether the information being shared was reliable or not
estimates.source_quote: We found that of the 47 educational videos, around 55% (n = 26) were classed as reliable whilst the remaining 45% (n = 21) were deemed unreliable.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 1 of 2; Table 1 'Creators of reliable and unreliable educational videos'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Single-author research letter; videos categorised by creator and content type and educational videos rated reliable/unreliable against NICE CG153 and NICE CKS. No number of coders, no independent double-coding and no reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: To carry out our study, we first searched TikTok using “#Psoriasis” and navigated our way to the hashtag section. From here, we selected the first 200 videos to include in our study.
estimates.notes: borderline=true because 'reliable/unreliable' is a guideline-concordance judgement rather than explicit true/false coding, so an incomplete-but-true video could in principle be marked unreliable; the paper's own framing is unambiguous ('TikTok is filled with considerable amounts of misinformation'; health/wellness gurus 'produce large amounts of misleading content') and the described unreliable content is advice to stop prescribed medication, so CONTENT rather than QUALITY. 21/47 = 44.7%; the paper states 'around 45%'. Denominator is the 47 educational videos, not all 134 (the other 87 are personal/humorous content that was never rated). Top-of-hashtag selection, hence denom_selection=curated.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: the likes comparison (reliable educational content 2 million likes vs unreliable 850,000, and one 400,000-like video claiming a causal link between psoriasis and a yeast) - these are engagement counts with no stated denominator, and converting them to a share would require a cross-category sum, which R8 forbids. Also not extracted: 49% of patient-created videos showing physical plaque removal (a behaviour depicted, not a veracity classification), and the creator-type shares (54% patients, 12% dermatologists, 11% gurus).

rob.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the first 200 videos in the TikTok #Psoriasis hashtag feed; 65 excluded as non-English and 1 as off-topic, leaving 134; creator type and content type coded; only the 47 educational videos were rated for reliability, against NICE CG153 and NICE CKS; single author, no double-coding or reliability statistic, search date not reported.
rob.item6_quote: Specifically for educational content, we used the NICE guidelines2 and NICE clinical knowledge summaries3 to determine whether the information being shared was reliable or not.
rob.item10_quote: We found that of the 47 educational videos, around 55% (n = 26) were classed as reliable whilst the remaining 45% (n = 21) were deemed unreliable.
